---
title: "Codec design"
subtitle: "Why quantize, delta-encode, and shuffle"
---

## The pipeline

1. **Origin-normalize** — subtract the first timestamp so tick values start near zero.
2. **Quantize** — round to integer ticks at a configurable resolution (default `100 µs`).
3. **Delta-encode** — store `d0 = 0, d_i = tick_i - tick_{i-1}` instead of absolute ticks.
4. **Narrow the dtype** — pick the smallest of `uint16 -> uint32 -> uint64` that holds the largest delta.
5. **Compress with Blosc(zstd, shuffle)** — the byte-shuffle filter regroups bytes by
   significance before Zstandard compression, which helps narrow integer/delta arrays
   compress far better than compressing the raw bytes directly.

## Why delta-encoding helps

Spike times are sorted. Absolute timestamps span the whole recording (high entropy,
wide dtype required), but successive differences between spikes are almost always
small — bounded by typical inter-spike intervals rather than recording duration. Small,
low-entropy integers compress dramatically better under Zstandard than wide,
high-entropy ones.

## Why quantize at all

Spike sorters resolve times to sample-rate precision (tens of microseconds), but most
downstream analyses (PSTHs, event alignment, correlation) don't need finer than
`~100 µs`. Quantizing before delta-encoding shrinks the deltas further and caps the
maximum error introduced to half a tick. This is the only lossy step in the pipeline —
everything else (delta-encoding, dtype narrowing, Blosc) is exactly invertible.

## Why the dtype fallback chain

A single insertion-wide delta encoding is only as good as its widest gap. A
recording with a long silent gap (a pause between sessions, a probe repositioning
break) could overflow `uint16` even though 99.9% of deltas are tiny. Rather than
force every recording onto a wide dtype "just in case", `encode_times` starts narrow
and only widens when a specific train actually needs it — recorded in `meta["dtype"]`,
so the choice is self-describing per train rather than a hardcoded assumption.

## Picking a quantization

This recipe was profiled and frozen for the IBL Brain-Wide Map `bwm_ephys` release at
`100 µs` as the preferred tradeoff between compact storage, decode speed, and fidelity
for reviewed BWM analyses — see the [benchmark](benchmark.qmd) page and the
[quantization how-to](../how-to/choose-quantization.qmd) for how to pick a value for
your own data instead of assuming `100 µs` is universally correct.
